https://classic107.com/articles/intermez.text: INTERMEZZO AT 1 P.M.: Celebrate week one of Folklorama with music inspired by five pavilions Each weekday at 1:00 p.m. this week, Intermezzo celebrates Winnipeg's favourite summer tradition by featuring orchestral masterpieces inspired by the cultures represented at Week One of Folklorama . Running from August 2–15 , Folklorama is the world's largest and longest-running multicultural festival, bringing together 45 cultural pavilions from across the globe. Visitors can enjoy authentic cuisine, vibrant dance, live music, cultural displays, and warm hospitality while travelling the world without ever leaving Winnipeg. Our musical journey mirrors several of the Week One pavilions currently welcoming visitors across the city. From the lush Celtic landscapes of Ireland to the majestic fjords of Scandinavia , the rich musical traditions of Poland , the heartfelt spirit of Ukraine , and the vibrant sounds of Romania , each day's featured work offers a deeper appreciation of the cultures being celebrated throughout Folklorama. Whether you're planning an evening at one of the pavilions or simply enjoying an afternoon of exceptional classical music, join us at 1:00 p.m. all this week for an unforgettable musical adventure. Monday, August 3 Irish Pavilion Featured Work: Symphony No. 3 "Irish" – Charles Villiers Stanford Performance: Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra conducted by David Lloyd-Jones Although born in Dublin in 1852, Charles Villiers Stanford spent much of his career in England, becoming one of the most influential composers and teachers of the late nineteenth century. His Third Symphony, completed in 1887, proudly embraces his Irish heritage. Rather than relying heavily on traditional folk tunes, Stanford captures the character of Ireland through sweeping melodies, lively dance rhythms, and lyrical writing that evokes the country's landscapes and spirit. The symphony helped establish him as one of Britain's leading composers and demonstrated that music inspired by national identity could stand alongside the great European symphonic tradition. Tuesday, August 4 Scandinavian Pavilion Featured Work: Symphonic Dances, Op. 64 – Edvard Grieg Performance: WDR Sinfonieorchester Köln conducted by Eivind Aadland Edvard Grieg remains Norway's best-known composer, and his Symphonic Dances represent one of his most accomplished orchestral works. Completed in 1898, the four dances are based on traditional Norwegian folk melodies collected by composer Ludvig Mathias Lindeman . Grieg transforms these rustic tunes into richly orchestrated concert music filled with brilliant colours, memorable melodies, and infectious rhythms. The work captures everything from energetic village celebrations to moments of quiet Nordic reflection, painting vivid musical pictures of Norway's landscapes and traditions. Polish Pavilion Featured Work: Violin Concerto No. 2 – Emil Młynarski Performance: Eugene Ugorski, violin, with the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra One of Poland's most distinguished musicians, Emil Młynarski enjoyed an international career as both violin virtuoso and conductor while also serving as director of the Warsaw Philharmonic. His Second Violin Concerto demonstrates a composer firmly rooted in the late Romantic tradition while embracing the expressive lyricism that characterizes much Polish music. Written for his own instrument, the concerto is filled with brilliant virtuosity, soaring melodies, and passages of remarkable emotional depth. Although overshadowed by better-known violin concertos of the era, the work has experienced a welcome revival in recent years thanks to outstanding modern recordings. Thursday, August 6 Ukraine Kyiv Pavilion Featured Work: Symphony No. 1 "From My Homeland" – Sergei Bortkiewicz Performance: BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra conducted by Martyn Brabbins Sergei Bortkiewicz was born in present-day Ukraine and lived through some of the most turbulent events of the twentieth century. Forced to flee his homeland during the Russian Revolution, he carried with him a profound sense of nostalgia that found expression throughout his music. His First Symphony, subtitled From My Homeland, is both a love letter to the country of his birth and an expression of longing for a place forever changed by history. Richly romantic in style, the symphony combines sweeping melodies, powerful orchestration, and moments of heartfelt lyricism that reflect both personal memory and national identity. Friday, August 7 Friday, August 7 Israeli Pavilion – Shalom Square Featured Work: Symphony No. 1 – Paul Ben-Haim Performance: Israel Philharmonic Orchestra conducted by Lahav Shani Paul Ben-Haim is considered one of the most important composers in the development of Israeli classical music. Born Paul Frankenburger in Germany in 1897, he immigrated to what was then Palestine in 1933, where he embraced his new home and helped create a distinct Israeli musical identity. His Symphony No. 1 , composed between 1939 and 1940, reflects a fascinating blend of European symphonic tradition and the sounds, rhythms, and colours of the Middle East. The work captures the composer’s connection to his adopted homeland, featuring expansive melodies, vibrant orchestration, and a sense of optimism and renewal. Whether you are visiting the pavilions in person or enjoying the journey from home, this week's Intermezzo offers the perfect soundtrack to the first week of Folklorama. From the passionate melodies of Ireland and the Nordic landscapes of Scandinavia to the rich traditions of Poland, Ukraine, and Romania, each selection celebrates the incredible diversity of cultures that make Winnipeg such a vibrant city. Join us every weekday at 1:00 p.m. from August 3–7 as we explore remarkable orchestral works inspired by the countries and communities being celebrated throughout Folklorama. It is a week of unforgettable music, fascinating stories, and a reminder that through the power of music, we can travel the world without ever leaving Winnipeg.
